---
title: "Bond Pricing: An Interactive Introduction"
description: "Use a two-year bond to understand present value and explore the price-yield relationship."
---

## The problem

Imagine buying a bond with a face value of **100**, a **5% annual coupon**, and **two years** until maturity. It pays **5** after the first year and **105** after the second year. How much should you pay today?

The answer depends on the market yield required by investors. We use annual compounding and assume both cash flows have the same yield.

## Derive the price from cash flows

A future payment is worth less than an identical payment today. Discount each cash flow at the required annual yield, $y$:

$$
P(y)=\frac{5}{1+y}+\frac{105}{(1+y)^2}
$$ {#eq-bond-price}

If $y=0.05$, the bond is worth exactly 100. The next experiment changes **only the yield**, keeping the cash flows fixed.

## Experiment: move the market yield

```{ojs}
viewof yieldPercent = Inputs.range([1, 12], {
  label: "Market yield (%)",
  value: 5,
  step: 0.5
})
```

```{ojs}
bondPrice = (percent) => {
  const y = percent / 100;
  return 5 / (1 + y) + 105 / ((1 + y) ** 2);
}
```

```{ojs}
currentPrice = bondPrice(yieldPercent);
html`<p style="font-size:1.2rem"><strong>Bond price:</strong> ${currentPrice.toFixed(2)} &nbsp; <span style="font-size:.85rem">at a yield of ${yieldPercent.toFixed(1)}%</span></p>`
```

```{ojs}
rates = Array.from({length: 111}, (_, i) => {
  const yieldValue = 1 + i * 0.1;
  return {yieldValue, price: bondPrice(yieldValue)};
});
Plot.plot({
  width: 680,
  height: 350,
  marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Market yield (%)"},
  y: {label: "Bond price"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(rates, {x: "yieldValue", y: "price", stroke: "#16877b", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleX([yieldPercent], {stroke: "#c27a30", strokeDasharray: "5,4"}),
    Plot.dot([{yieldValue: yieldPercent, price: currentPrice}],
      {x: "yieldValue", y: "price", fill: "#c27a30", r: 6}),
    Plot.ruleY([100], {stroke: "gray", strokeDasharray: "3,5"})
  ]
})
```

## What did you observe?

When the yield increases, the present value of the future cash flows decreases. When the yield decreases, their present value increases. This is the **inverse price-yield relationship**.

The price is **not** changing because the issuer changed the promised payments. It changes because the *required return* changed.

## Next step: quantify sensitivity

The price-yield curve is not a straight line. For a small yield change, we can approximate the local effect with a derivative. This is the motivation for [Duration](duration.qmd).

> **Scope:** The model uses annual compounding, fixed payments, a single yield, and no default risk or accrued-interest adjustment. It is an educational example rather than a market pricing engine.
